title: How Are We Saved?
subtitle: Grace, election, and the human will, with each serious view stated by its own best defenders
triageNote: This doctrine divides denominations, not the faith itself. A Calvinist and an Arminian who both trust Christ for salvation are brothers. They will worship in different buildings. They will sometimes argue late into the night. But they are saved by the same grace they disagree about describing.
question: When a person is saved, who does what, and in what order? Does God choose us before we could choose anything, and then work in us the very willingness by which we come? Or does God offer grace widely and genuinely, and then wait on a free human yes that He has made possible but does not compel? When you came to faith, were you the one who reached out across the dark toward a God you had begun to want, or were you the one who had already been found and carried before you understood what was happening to you? The whole debate sits inside that single experience nearly every believer has had, the experience of looking back at your own conversion and not being able to say with certainty whether you found God or God found you. This is not a new question. It runs from Augustine arguing with Pelagius in the early fifth century, through the medieval schoolmen, into the Reformation and the long quarrel between the followers of Calvin and the followers of Arminius after the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, and it continues in living churches today. The question matters because it touches the most intimate thing about you, the moment grace became real, and it asks who was the actor in that moment and who was the one acted upon.
whyItMatters:
If you are new to faith, you may wonder why grown people who love the same Lord have fought over this for five hundred years and longer. Here is the honest answer. How you understand salvation shapes how you pray, how you evangelize, how you handle the friend who walks away from Christ, and how you sleep at night when your own faith feels thin. If God chose you and holds you, your security rests entirely outside yourself, in a decision He made about you before you existed. If your free response matters in a way that can be lost, then your daily yes carries real weight, and real warning, and the urgency of the New Testament's commands to endure makes a different kind of sense. Neither of these is a small thing to carry into a hospital room or a deathbed.

It also shapes how you read your own story. The believer who is convinced God did everything will fall to their knees in gratitude for a rescue they did not earn and could not have begun. The believer who is convinced they freely responded will feel the dignity of a love that was offered and not forced, a love that honored them enough to let them say no. Both are trying to protect something precious, and you will not understand the people in your own congregation until you see what each is afraid of losing. One side is protecting the sheer freeness of grace, the conviction that if salvation depends in any final way on me then I have a sliver of credit and grace is no longer grace (Romans 11:6). The other side is protecting the goodness and sincerity of God, the conviction that a God who commands all to repent and grieves over those who will not (Ezekiel 18:32) must be offering something real to all of them. These are not academic worries. They are pastoral worries, the kind that surface when a mother asks whether her wandering son was ever truly chosen, or when a doubting saint asks whether his faltering grip means he was never held at all. How you answer will change what you can honestly say to that mother and that saint.

positions.name: Calvinism (Reformed)
positions.inOneLine: Salvation is God's work from first to last. He chooses, He calls, He gives the faith by which we believe, and He keeps us to the end.
positions.bestCase:
Start with what you actually were before grace, because everything turns on this. The Bible does not say you were sick and needing a doctor's help, or drowning and needing a hand to grab. It says you were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), that you were by nature a child of wrath, that the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God and is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14). A dead man does not cooperate with his own resurrection. Lazarus did not meet Christ halfway out of the tomb. He was called, and the call created the life it commanded. So when God saves, He does not stand at the door of a will that remains free to refuse Him forever and knock and hope. He gives a new heart of flesh in place of the heart of stone (Ezekiel 36:26), and the new heart wants Him. This is what we mean by regeneration, the new birth of John 3, God making a dead person alive so that faith becomes possible at all. Regeneration comes first in the order of salvation, and faith is its fruit, not its cause. Augustine saw this against Pelagius sixteen centuries ago when he prayed, command what you will and give what you command, and the Reformers recovered it.

We hold to monergism, a word that simply means one worker. In the decisive moment of being made alive, God acts and we receive. We do not add the last crucial piece. If we did, then in the end the difference between the saved man and the lost man beside him, who heard the same sermon, would be something in the saved man, some better choice, some softer heart he managed to produce on his own. And then heaven would have one small room left for boasting, and Paul's question would have an answer, what do you have that you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7). Grace that depends finally on my decision is grace I can take partial credit for, and Scripture will not let me. Salvation is by grace through faith, and even that is not your own doing, it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Election, then, is God's choice before the foundation of the world to set His saving love on a people (Ephesians 1:4-5). It is not God looking down the corridor of time, seeing who would choose Him, and ratifying their foreseen choice, because that would make the human choice the real cause of election and empty the doctrine of its comfort. It is unconditional. Paul presses the point as hard as it can be pressed. God chose Jacob and not Esau before either was born and before either had done anything good or bad, so that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of Him who calls (Romans 9:11-13). This is humbling, and it is meant to be. The Synod of Dort defended exactly this against the Remonstrants in 1619, and the great Reformed confessions have carried it since.

And because salvation is His work from first to last, it cannot finally fail. Those whom He foreknew He predestined, those He predestined He called, those He called He justified, those He justified He glorified (Romans 8:29-30). The chain does not break in the middle, and no link has fewer members than the others. This is perseverance, the certainty that He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6), the certainty that no one can snatch Christ's sheep out of His hand (John 10:28-29). Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your grip on God, which trembles. It rests on the strength of His grip on you, which does not.

We know the hard part, and we will not pretend it away. We know it sounds as if God could save everyone and chooses not to, and we know the weight of that. But we would rather sit in reverent silence before a hard truth that exalts God's freedom than soften it to fit what we find comfortable. Paul himself anticipated your exact objection, why does He still find fault, for who can resist His will, and he did not resolve it with a tidy theodicy. He answered with a question, who are you, O man, to answer back to God (Romans 9:19-20). We let that question stand, and we worship.

positions.name: Arminianism (Wesleyan)
positions.inOneLine: God's grace goes first and makes a free response possible, but that grace can be received or resisted, because love that cannot be refused is not love.
positions.bestCase:
Let us clear away the worst caricature right at the start, because nearly everyone who attacks us is attacking a man who does not exist. We do not believe you save yourself. We do not believe you take the first step. We believe with the whole church that you were dead in sin and could not move one inch toward God under your own power. Arminius himself, and John Wesley after him, affirmed total depravity in language as strong as anything in Calvin. Wesley wrote that natural man is altogether corrupt and that there is no health in him. So the disagreement is not about whether man is helpless. We grant that fully. The whole question is what God does about that helplessness, and to whom.

Our answer is prevenient grace, grace that comes before. The word prevenient simply means going ahead of you. Before you ever sought God, before you had a flicker of desire for Him, God was already at work, drawing through the cross (John 12:32), convicting by the Spirit (John 16:8), loosening the chains that sin had locked on the will, so that for the first time in your life you were genuinely able to say yes, and genuinely able to say no. This is not you producing faith out of some native goodness you retained. It is God graciously restoring enough freedom that a real response, for or against Him, becomes possible. The grace is entirely a gift, unearned and undeserved. The response is genuinely yours, and that is the whole point.

Why do we insist the response can be refused? Because the Scriptures are saturated with God's grief over people who would not come. Jesus stood over the city and wept, how often I wanted to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). Stephen, full of the Spirit, told the council you always resist the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51). The Lord stretched out His hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (Romans 10:21). If grace cannot in any sense be resisted, these tears and these rebukes become a kind of theater, and we cannot read them that way. We take God at His plain word when He says He desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4), and that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). We cannot bring ourselves to believe that behind that revealed desire stands a hidden decree willing the opposite for most of the human race.

This is synergism, a word that means working together, and it is the most misunderstood word in this whole debate. We do not mean equal partners. We never mean that. God provides the grace, the power, the initiative, the atonement, the drawing, the regeneration, the entire substance of salvation. We contribute nothing whatsoever except the empty hands of faith that receive what He alone supplies, and even those hands He pries open. But the receiving is real, and it is ours, and it could have been withheld by us, or it would not be receiving at all. Election, on our reading, is God's gracious choice to save those who are in Christ through faith. He foreknew His people, set His love on them, and that love was wide enough to have embraced anyone at all who would come.

Why do we hold all this, finally? We are protecting the revealed character of God. We cannot worship, though we would still obey, a God who brings persons into being specifically in order to pass them by, when their salvation would have cost Him nothing beyond the price He had already paid in full. The cross was for the world (John 3:16), Christ is the propitiation not for our sins only but for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2:2). We would far rather carry the mystery of why some refuse a love that was really offered to them than the heavier mystery of a love that, for most, was never actually offered at all.

positions.name: Provisionism (Traditionalist / Southern Baptist)
positions.inOneLine: God has provided salvation for everyone in the cross, and the gospel itself, heard and believed, is the means by which the lost are made able to respond.
positions.bestCase:
We are often lumped in with the Arminians, and on the big result we agree with them, but we differ on the machinery in a way that matters, so hear us on our own terms. We do not build our view on prevenient grace understood as a separate, invisible operation poured uniformly into every human heart at birth. We build it on the gospel itself. The word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12). So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). When the good news is genuinely preached, it carries within it the very power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16). You do not need to posit a hidden prior surgery on the soul to explain how a sinner can believe. You need the cross preached truly and the Spirit working through that preached word, which is exactly what the New Testament shows happening from Pentecost forward.

On the human condition we take sin with complete seriousness, and we resent the suggestion that we do not. People apart from Christ are lost, condemned already (John 3:18), incapable of saving themselves or earning a thing. But we do not read the deadness of Ephesians 2 as a metaphysical inability to respond to the gospel when God Himself calls through it. We read the Bible's relentless, sincere commands to repent and believe (Acts 17:30, Mark 1:15) as real commands issued to real people who, when the gospel comes to them in power, are genuinely enabled to obey. We do not think God mocks the lost by commanding what He knows they are constitutionally unable to do and then condemning them for not doing it.

On election we hold that God's saving choice is corporate and conditional. From eternity God determined to save a people in Christ, and whoever is in Christ by faith is chosen in Him (Ephesians 1:4, in Him). The election is real, but it is election in Christ, not a pre-creation list of named individuals sorted for heaven and hell. We simply do not find in Scripture the picture of a God who, before any person existed, selected some for glory and left the rest with no genuine opportunity to be saved. We find instead a God whose provision in the cross is universal, whose call goes out indiscriminately to all, and who actually saves all who trust His Son and no others.

This is the view that Southern Baptists put into words in their 2012 statement, A Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God's Plan of Salvation, which tried to say plainly what generations of believers had always assumed from the pulpit and the altar call: that Christ died for every person, that the offer of salvation is sincere to every hearer, and that no one finally perishes because God secretly withheld from him the ability to come.

We hold this, in the end, because we want the invitation to be honest. When we stand at the front of a sanctuary and say whosoever will may come, let him take the water of life without price (Revelation 22:17), we mean it without crossed fingers and without a mental footnote that it really applies only to a hidden few. We are not protecting human pride. We are protecting the plain sense of a thousand gospel pleadings and the integrity of the God who makes them. The Lord is not willing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). We take that sentence to mean what it says.

biblicalEvidence.summary: You were dead in trespasses, and God made you alive together with Christ. Salvation is by grace through faith, and even that is not your own doing, it is the gift of God, so that no one may boast.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians agree we were dead and that grace is the gift. They argue the gift offered can still be received or declined, and that the faith spoken of as a gift is the gift made possible by prevenient grace, not an irresistible deposit. Provisionists read deadness as guilt and helplessness to self-rescue, not as inability to respond to the preached gospel.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Before the twins had done anything, God said the older will serve the younger, that His purpose of election might stand. He has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills. Who are you to answer back to God?
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians and Provisionists argue Paul is discussing God's choice of nations and roles in redemptive history, Israel and the nations, not the eternal destiny of individuals. Jacob and Esau stand for peoples. The mercy in view is God's freedom to set the terms of salvation, which He has set as faith in Christ open to all.

biblicalEvidence.summary: All that the Father gives me will come to me. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And those given to Jesus He will raise on the last day.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians point out the same chapter says the Father draws and then adds, in John 12:32, that Jesus lifted up will draw all people. They take the drawing as wide and resistible. Provisionists stress that the drawing happens through the Father's word and teaching, verse 45, everyone who has heard and learned comes, which they read as the gospel doing its work, not a selective inward pull.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children together, and you were not willing. Jesus expresses a real desire. It meets a real refusal.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists note the verse contrasts the children Jesus wanted to gather with the leaders who would not let Him, so the unwillingness may belong to the leaders blocking the people. They also distinguish God's revealed desire that all repent from His hidden decree, holding both without collapsing one into the other.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God our Savior desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists argue all here means all kinds of people, kings and commoners, Jew and Gentile, not every individual without exception. In 2 Peter, they read the any and the all as the elect, those God is patiently gathering, so that none of His own will be lost before the end.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Those God foreknew He predestined, and those He predestined He called, justified, and glorified. The unbroken chain holds from eternity past to glory.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians read foreknew in its relational sense, God set His love beforehand on those He knew would be His in Christ, and the chain describes what is true of all who are in Christ by faith. They note glorified is stated of a group, a people, not a proof that no individual can fall away.

biblicalEvidence.summary: If you confess with your mouth and believe in your heart, you will be saved. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists fully affirm the call goes out to all and that faith comes by hearing. They add that the effectual call within the outward call is what makes some hearers believe, so the preaching is God's ordinary means, not a power that works the same in every heart that hears it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Those once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Holy Spirit, if they fall away, cannot be restored to repentance. A sober warning that real participants can apostatize.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists read this as a hypothetical warning God uses as a means to keep His people persevering, or as describing those who tasted the things of God outwardly without ever being truly born again, as 1 John 2:19 says, they went out from us because they were not of us. The warning is real. And it is effective precisely because it produces the perseverance it commands.

biblicalEvidence.summary: When the Gentiles heard this they rejoiced, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Belief follows divine appointment.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Provisionists and some Arminians argue the verb can carry the sense of those who had set themselves toward, or were disposed to, eternal life, or that the appointment is to the offer now extended to Gentiles in redemptive history. The point of the verse, they say, is the opening of salvation to the nations. Not a roster of predestined individuals.

weighing:
What follows is my own reading, and I want to be plain about its status. It is offered as one pastor's judgment, formed over years of preaching and burying the dead, and not as a verdict the church has settled or ever will settle this side of glory. Hold it loosely, more loosely than I hold it myself. People far holier and far sharper than I am have spent whole lives in each of these camps. Augustine and Calvin and Edwards on one side, Wesley and Arminius and a great cloud of faithful witnesses on the others, and I have stood at the graves of saints from all three and watched them go home to the same Christ.

When I sit with the whole of Scripture and not with my preferences, the texts that exalt God's initiative seem to me to carry more weight than I once wanted them to. Ephesians 2, John 6, Romans 8 and 9, and Acts 13:48 keep pressing in the same direction, and I have grown tired of explaining them all away. The dead do not raise themselves. The love that saved me was reaching across the dark for me long before I had the sense to reach back, and the more honestly I examine my own conversion the less I can find any good decision of mine that deserves the credit. The instinct behind the Reformed reading, that grace is so free and so deep it leaves no room at all for boasting and no room for anxiety either, rings true to the actual texture of being saved, where every honest backward look turns into thanksgiving and not into self-congratulation.

And yet I cannot make the tears of Matthew 23 disappear, and I will not try, and I distrust any system that needs them gone. When Jesus stands over the city and grieves the ones who would not come, He means it, with everything in Him. The Arminian and the Provisionist are guarding something I dare not lose, that God's invitations are sincere all the way down, that His grief is honest and not staged, and that the lost are not props in a drama that condemned them before they had drawn a single breath. The strongest Calvinists I trust, men like John Murray and J.I. Packer, hold the free and sincere offer of the gospel together with the sovereign decree and refuse to soften either one into the other, and that uneasy double grip is where I try to stand, and often fail.

So here is my tentative resting place, which I commend to no one as a law. I lean toward grace going first and going deepest, toward the conviction that if I am saved at all it is because He carried me the whole way and not because I supplied the deciding inch. But I refuse to use that conviction as a tool to flatten the mystery of why some refuse a real offer, and I refuse to speak of the lost as though their refusal were not truly and damnably their own. The deepest knot, how God's full sovereignty and full human responsibility are both completely true at once, I will not pretend to untie, because the apostle who saw furthest into it did not untie it either. Paul reached the edge of this very question and broke into doxology, oh the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, how unsearchable His judgments (Romans 11:33). He worshiped in front of the mystery rather than dissolving it. I have come to think that is the only honest place to end.
charitableDisagreement:
If you hold a different view than the one I lean toward, here is what I most want you to hear from me, and to carry into your next argument about this. The thoughtful Arminian is not soft on grace and is not quietly exalting human pride. He is defending the goodness and sincerity of God against a picture he finds genuinely unbearable, and he reads the same Bible you do, on his knees, with the same Spirit. The thoughtful Calvinist is not a fatalist who has secretly concluded that evangelism is pointless. He preaches the gospel to every creature precisely because preaching is the appointed means by which God calls His own out of death, and he weeps over the lost as hard as any man alive, because Whitefield wept and Spurgeon wept and they believed every word of this. The thoughtful Provisionist is not dodging the hard texts of Romans 9 or running from the depth of human sin. He is fighting to keep the gospel invitation honest at the altar, so that the words whosoever will are not a cruelty. Each of these believers is guarding a real treasure that the Scriptures plainly contain, and each one fears, sometimes with reason, that the others will let it slip.

Is this a hill to die on? No. It is a hill to think hard on, to pray over, to argue about late into the night with people you love and then take the same bread and the same cup beside the next morning. The line that actually divides the faith from unbelief is not Calvin from Wesley, and it never was. It is whether you trust Christ crucified and risen for your salvation at all, or whether you are still trusting yourself. On that question, all three of these views stand together on the same side of the only chasm that finally matters, and they will sing the same songs in the same heaven. Do not let a second-order debate, however serious, fool you into treating a blood-bought brother as if he were an enemy of the cross.

relatedDebates.note: For whom did Christ die? Calvinists who hold particular redemption say the cross actually secured salvation for the elect, otherwise Christ died for many who are never saved and the cross is a payment that does not pay. Arminians and Provisionists hold a general atonement, that Christ truly died for all (1 John 2:2, 1 Timothy 2:6), and that the cross provides salvation for everyone while applying it only to those who believe. Many Reformed Baptists take a middle path, sometimes called sufficient for all and efficient for the elect.

relatedDebates.topic: Perseverance versus the possibility of apostasy
relatedDebates.note: Can a truly saved person be finally lost? Calvinists say no, the elect will persevere because God preserves them (John 10:28-29, Philippians 1:6), and those who fall away show they were never truly regenerate (1 John 2:19). Classical Arminians and many Provisionists say a genuine believer can, through settled unbelief, fall away (Hebrews 6, Hebrews 10:26-29). Note that most Southern Baptists affirm eternal security even while rejecting unconditional election, so the camps do not line up as neatly as people assume.

relatedDebates.topic: Justification and the New Perspective on Paul
relatedDebates.note: Justification is God declaring a guilty person righteous in Christ. The Reformation taught it is by faith alone, apart from works, with Christ's righteousness credited to us. The New Perspective, associated with E.P. Sanders, James Dunn, and N.T. Wright, argues that Paul's fight against works of the law was less about earning salvation by good deeds and more about the badges of Jewish identity, circumcision and food laws, that wrongly excluded Gentiles. Critics like John Piper warn this can blur the credited righteousness of Christ that gives believers their security. Defenders reply that they are recovering Paul's actual first century setting, not denying grace. This one cuts across the Calvinist and Arminian divide entirely.
